passage: Reading circle at a school in Leh. Dolma, five, stood up to say her name and her favourite animal. "My name is D... Dolma," she began, and her voice wobbled on the last word. "My... favourite is... a snow leopard." Her voice shook and her eyes shone. Teacher Anirban said, "It's normal to feel wobbly when you talk in front of everyone. Take your time." Dolma took a breath and finished, "Because it's brave and quiet." The class clapped softly.

qa.q: What is Dolma's favourite animal?
qa.a: Her favourite is a snow leopard.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been feeling when her voice wobbled and her eyes shone?
qa.a: She was probably nervous or close to crying because she was speaking in front of everyone. She may also have felt shy.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped Dolma?
qa.a: Anirban named the wobbly feeling as normal and told her to take her time, instead of telling her to stop.

qa.q: How might the class feel as Dolma's voice shakes?
qa.a: Some may feel sympathy, and their soft clapping shows they were on her side.

grounding: A child's voice wobbles before a class from nerves, and naming it kindly as normal helps more than telling her to stop.

passage: I was at the back of Class 1 in our Gwalior school when Rajni stood up to read her poem. Her voice cracked on the second line and she stopped, blinking hard. Some of us shifted in our seats. The teacher, Jasleen, said quietly, "Lots of people feel wobbly when they speak to the class. It's normal." Rajni started again, more slowly, her voice still shaky, and she reached the end. I don't know if she was nervous or nearly crying, but afterwards she sat with her hands tight in her lap.

qa.q: Where was Rajni when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She stood up to read her poem in front of the Gwalior school's Class 1.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She might have been nervous or about to cry, and she blinked hard and sat with tight hands afterwards. The narrator cannot tell which.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do next to help Rajni feel safe?
qa.a: Jasleen can keep saying that feeling wobbly is normal and let Rajni take her time when she speaks.

qa.q: How might the other children feel watching Rajni?
qa.a: Some may feel uncomfortable and shift in their seats, though a kind word from the teacher helps them be patient.

grounding: A child's voice cracks before a class from nerves, and an observer sees it and a teacher names it kindly.

passage:
Monday: At show-and-tell, Samir stood up with his toy train. “This is my… my…” His voice cracked and quavered. His eyes filled. Nirmala Ma'am knelt. “Your voice feels wobbly. That's normal when lots of people are looking.” Samir nodded and sat down.
Wednesday: He tried again, holding Ma'am's hand. “This is my train.” Still a bit shaky.
Friday: Samir stood alone. His voice wobbled on the first word, then steadied. “And it goes choo choo!” The class clapped.

qa.q: What did Samir bring to show-and-tell?
qa.a: His toy train.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when his voice cracked on Monday?
qa.a: He was nervous about speaking in front of the class and close to tears.

qa.q: What helped Samir more than telling him to stop?
qa.a: Nirmala Ma'am named his wobbly voice kindly as normal, and let him try again with her hand to hold.

qa.q: How might the class see Samir on Friday?
qa.a: They saw a friend proudly sharing his train, which is why they clapped.

grounding: Over a week, a child's quavering voice before the class is named kindly, and he gradually speaks with more confidence.

passage: The annual-day rehearsal was a mess of drums, a broken microphone and only ten minutes left. Yusuf stepped up to say his one line. “I am the… the… moon.” His voice wobbled and squeaked. Some older boys laughed. Jomon Sir stopped the music. “Hey. A wobbly voice is normal. Lots of people feel wobbly before a show.” He turned to the older boys. “Nobody laughs at wobbles here.” He gave Yusuf a nod. Yusuf took a breath. “I am the moon.” Clearer this time.

qa.q: What was Yusuf's one line?
qa.a: “I am the moon.”

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when his voice wobbled and squeaked?
qa.a: He was nervous about saying his line in a noisy, rushed rehearsal, and the laughter may have made him feel embarrassed.

qa.q: Which choice by Jomon Sir worked, and why?
qa.a: He paused, named the wobble as normal and stopped the laughing, which let Yusuf try again with more confidence.

qa.q: What is it like for Yusuf when the older boys laugh?
qa.a: It likely feels humiliating and makes his voice even wobblier.

grounding: A child's quavering voice in a rushed rehearsal is named kindly as normal, helping him more than telling him to stop.

passage: At the Mothers' Day assembly in the city school, each child read one line to their mother. Himani's mother was on a night shift at the hospital and couldn't come. When it was her turn, Himani's voice cracked. “My mummy… is…” She stopped, lips trembling. Sunaina Ma'am came to stand beside her. “It's okay to feel wobbly. Your mummy will hear it later.” She held up her phone to record. Himani's voice still shook. “My mummy is brave.” The hall went quiet, then clapped warmly.

qa.q: Where was Himani's mother?
qa.a: On a night shift at the hospital.

qa.q: What does Himani's cracking voice suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was sad that her mother couldn't come and about to cry, as well as nervous in front of the hall.

qa.q: What did Sunaina Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She named the wobbly feeling kindly and offered to record the line, so Himani's mother could still hear it.

qa.q: How might Himani's mother feel watching the recording later?
qa.a: She would likely feel moved and proud to hear her daughter call her brave.

grounding: A child's voice cracks while speaking before the school, and her teacher names the feeling kindly.

passage:
"Shalini, will you say your poem for us?"

Shalini stood up. "The... the moon is round, the..." Her voice cracked and wobbled. She stopped, chin trembling.

"Take your time," said Disha Ma'am gently. "Your voice sounds a bit wobbly. That's normal when lots of people are listening. Mine does it too sometimes."

"Really?"

"Really. Want to take one big breath? I can say the first line with you."

"Okay."

"The moon is round..." they said together.

Shalini's voice steadied. "...the stars are bright."

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am offer to say with Shalini?
qa.a: The first line.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when her voice cracked and her chin trembled?
qa.a: She was most likely nervous about speaking in front of the class, and close to tears. Her surprised "Really?" suggests she felt relieved to hear it happens to adults too.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Disha Ma'am named the wobbly voice kindly, said it was normal, and offered a breath and the first line together, which steadied Shalini more than telling her to stop.

qa.q: What would change if Disha Ma'am had said, "Stop mumbling, speak up"?
qa.a: Shalini would probably have felt more embarrassed and might have cried or sat down without finishing the poem.

grounding: It shows a young child's voice cracking while reciting in class and a teacher kindly naming the wobble, which helps more than telling her to stop.
